newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan in Washington - money and "black helicopters".
newsitem.headline: Annan in Washington - money and "black helicopters".

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, who owes his job to Washington, was planning to go to the U.S. capital on Wednesday to tell an array of officials, including President Bill Clinton, how much they owe the world body he heads.

The trip follows at least two years of relentless criticism of the United Nations, from conservatives contending the world body has too much power to radical militia imagining black U.N. helicopters swooping down on lawnchairs.

Annan has said several times that his first year in office would be a "time for healing," a reference to the scorn heaped on the world body and his predecessor Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt, driven from office by the Clinton administration at the end of his five-year term.
Annan, who served in the U.N. system for more than 30 years and was in charge of peacekeeping, was a favourite of the Clinton administration.

Soft-spoken, with considerable charm and frankness, the 58-year-old Ghanian, who took office on Jan. 1, planned to try making his case to leading senators and congressmen that the United States needs the United Nations and vice versa.
And this meant paying the $1.3 billion debt owed by Washington that has crippled the world body and caused sharp criticism from Europeans who foot the bill.

"He has only a few months to cement the relationship and get the United States to really take its place among U.N. members and not shoot from the sidelines," said one senior official. "It is a healing time but not a long one."
Clinton proposed paying the debt by 1999, albeit with conditions. But whether the Republican-dominated Congress, which cut non-defence foreign aid to a bare minimlum, will agree was another question.

Annan was to begin his visit on Wednesday afternoon and on Thursday see Clinton, Secretary of State-designate Madeleine Albright and National Security Council chief Sandy Berger, among others. He was scheduled to leave Washington on Friday.

In attempting to shore up the U.N. relationship with Congress, Annan was to see a host of legislators including House Speaker Newt Gingrich, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott and North Carolina Senator Jesse Helms, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

But the wide gap between Democrats and Republicans was illustrated clearly in Helms' article in the Foreign Affairs magazine six months ago in which he advocated the United States withdraw from the United Nations unless its budget is slashed far more than anticipated so far.
Annan, since his election, touted reform and restructing as a top priority and planned to come up with wide-ranging proposals in the next six months.

But he pointedly said reform did not mean massive or "arbitrary" cuts in vital programmes. And some nations, like Japan, believed reform should not mean any lowering of dues, but release of funds for development to poor countries.

Since many of the bodies in the U.N. system were not under the control of the secretary-general but funded by voluntary contributions from member states, Annan's influence on wide-ranging restructuring was limited and dependent on approval by the 185-member General Assembly.

But since the Clinton administration faulted Boutros-Ghali for allegedly not paying enough attention to reform, Annan was left with an albatross of massive change in order to get the United States to participate fully in the United Nations.
"It is up to the member states to define what they want the United Nations to be and to do -- to outline their vision of the goals they want us to attain and to set new priorities," he said.
